newsitem.title: GERMANY: One-off convergence not enough for EMU-Duisenberg.
newsitem.headline: One-off convergence not enough for EMU-Duisenberg.

text.p: Dutch central bank chief Wim Duisenberg said on Wednesday countries would not be allowed to join European monetary union (EMU) through a one-off fulfilment of entry conditions set in the Maastricht treaty.

Duisenberg, who starts a new job as head of the European Monetary Institute this summer, said budget plans would also be taken into account by European leaders when they meet in spring 1998 to review the performance this year of contenders.
"When we evaluate convergence in March or April 1998, we will know not just the numbers for 1997, but also for 1998 and probably for 1999," he told Germany's Wirtschaftswoche weekly.
"If a country has a 1997 budget of 2.9 percent of GDP and parliament has decided on a deficit of four percent for 1998, then it cannot join monetary union," he added.

The remarks made by Duisenberg, a front-runner to take over as head of the planned European central bank which would evolve from the EMI after monetary union in 1999, were released ahead of publication in the magazine.

Duisenberg stressed that meeting the Maastricht treaty's budget deficit target of three percent of GDP had to be sustainable. The treaty sets 1997 as the decisive year for countries seeking to join the launch of the euro currency.
"The convergence criteria must be met, not just in 1997, but in the medium term. It won't help to prettify the books for one year," he told the magazine.
And, if the European Commission accepts the massaging of figures, then the EMI will use its own figures to decide which countries are fit to join the EMU starting line-up, he said.
Duisenberg said the Maastricht treaty did offer room for interpretation in meeting the convergence criteria, and said that a "critical mass of countries" should join at the outset.
That group would include at least Germany, France and the Netherlands, he said.
Duisenberg added that a delay to the EMU project was "very unlikely and dangerous."

"If there is a delay, the treaty would have to be renegotiated -- in 15 parliaments. Then we would not just be talking about the date, but every land would have its own special wishes," he told Wirtschaftswoche.
Duisenberg said he had no second thoughts about his candidacy, and rejected as "rubbish" reports of a secret deal between Bonn and Paris to push forward a French candidate.
